"At which point on the curve $x{y}^{2}=3-2y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $i?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{y}^{2}+2y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,j \\  & =(2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{y}^{2}+2y & =3\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+2y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=3.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+2y)\,j \\  & =(2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $i,$ we must have $t\cdot i=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot i & =0 \\ ((2xy+2)\,i-{y}^{2}\,j)\cdot i & =0 \\ 2xy+2 & =0 \\ xy+1 & =0 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-\frac{1}{x}$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x{y}^{2} & =3-2y \\ x{(-\frac{1}{x})}^{2} & =3-2(-\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{1}{x} & =3+\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & =-3 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

\nabla f(x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0 \rangle  = 0.

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(12x-2{y}^{2})\text{ }i+(4y-4xy)\text{ }j \\ ∇\,f(3,3) & =(12(3)-2(3)^{2})i+(4(3)-4(3)(3))j \\  & =18\,i-24\,j \\  & =⟨18,-24⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the level curve that passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)=(3,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(3,3)\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨18,-24⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can leave our answer in this form. Or, if we want to leave our final answer in Cartesian form, we expand the dot product and simplify:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = 6xy+3y^2 - y + 3x^2 ,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=7.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(x,y) = f_y(x,y) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x,y) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,j \\  & =(6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{j},$ we must have $\mathbf t \cdot \mathbf j = 0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -6y-6x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6x(-x)+3(-x)^{2} & =7+(-x)-3{x}^{2} \\ -6{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =7-x-3{x}^{2} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

[{:db/id 17592186125292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125733 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
$$

 at the point $P(3,1).$

To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Let's start by defining 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.
$$

Then, the given ellipse is the level curve  $f(x,y)=1.$

Now, we know that $\nabla \! f(3,1)$ is a vector that's normal to the level curve $f(x,y)= 1$ at $P(3,1).$ So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at $P.$

![](images/3d/3dc75e8fd4083af1bf90f46b2e875d5d552bffdc5c1cfaeabebef70f79f00828.png)

Suppose that $(x,y)$ is any point on that tangent line. Then $\mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle$ is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So $\mathbf v$ must be also orthogonal to $\nabla f(3,1),$ and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

$$
\nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.
$$

Now, computing $\nabla\! f$ and evaluating it at the point $P(3,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{x}{6},\frac{y}{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(3,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(3,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(y-1) & =0 \\ (x-3)+(y-1) & =0 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9dede8-0672-56eb-9084-cf581e3fb05f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2496 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7cc9655e-83bb-5f85-8c20-add1d27fb5e0" :step/math-academy-id 11184 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125464}} {:db/id 17592186125293 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124454 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124258 :question/id #uuid "a01560be-9023-593a-87d3-7412f3b208a3" :question/math-academy-id "e-3362"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5ae7e9c8-60e9-5f5e-afbf-1de6bb01bf07" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050027}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124979} {:db/id 17592186125075} {:db/id 17592186265823} {:db/id 17592186265826} {:db/id 17592186339099} {:db/id 17592186388076} {:db/id 17592186393208}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Tangent Line to a Level Curve"} :step/id #uuid "204027bd-d606-5131-82eb-717c2823cc14" :step/math-academy-id 11185 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125294}} {:db/id 17592186125294 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125734 :tutorial/content "Given a level curve $f(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0),$ a **tangent vector** is

$$

Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
